Mark Selby, the champion of the past two years, has been comprehensively beaten in the first round, 10-4 by Joe Perry. Ronnie O’Sullivan had to mount a mighty comeback himself, winning seven of the final eight frames to knock out Stephen Maguire 10-7. The opening weekend has already made the matter of who will claim the title an open one but it is not the only intriguing question at the Crucible this year.
Two weeks ago the sporting impresario Barry Hearn, who among other things has a controlling interest in the commercial operations of snooker’s governing body, announced he would be raising the prize money for a 147 maximum at the Crucible this year. The bonus, which had been based on a slightly complicated rollover system with a minimum reward of £5,000, will now default to £40,000. It is a big raise to counter a striking anomaly: in recent years snooker has gone 147‑loopy everywhere bar the world championship.
The basics of the snooker maximum require a player to make a clean sweep of the table, with every red that is potted being followed by a black. Established in the 1870s, with the first world championship taking place in 1927, snooker’s first recorded maximum came in 1955. It was scored by Joe Davis, the 15‑times world champion, and took two years before it was officially recognised. The first maximum in professional competition, meanwhile, did not come until 1982 when Steve Davis made the score in the Lada Classic in Oldham. To commemorate his accomplishment Davis was presented with a Lada with the customised numberplate of SD 147.
The story of the snooker maximum accelerated from that point. To date there have been 139 scores of 147 in professional snooker. Of that total 70 have come since the turn of the decade and three have come in the past four weeks. The Chinese player Liang Wenbo scored one in world championship qualifying and nearly reached another two frames later, only to fail on the final black.
O’Sullivan has the most 147s of any player, 14. The total includes the most feted maximum of all, scored against Mick Price in the first round of the 1997 world championship, a feat which took five minutes and 20 seconds to complete. When Sullivan made that break he was rewarded with a bonus of £147,000. Given the increasing frequency of the achievement, it is perhaps not surprising the prize money shrank. But there has not been a maximum at the world championship since Stephen Hendry cleaned the table against Stuart Bingham in 2012. The appetite to see an end to the barren run even led to O’Sullivan being suspected of having swerved one on purpose last year. Potting a pink after the final red when – in some eyes – it was possible for him to have screwed back for the black, Sullivan’s actions were deemed a protest against the insubstantial prize pot.

Some shooters, especially the ones who use an English war bow which is like 120 pounds, like to hold the arrow back and exert all their strength in pulling it. They normally go up to the second knuckle from the finger tips. However, it is not always recommended to use the second knuckles. If you are using a 50 pound bow, you can use the first row of knuckles from the tip of your fingers.
That gives you plenty of lock in pulling it back and it’s very comfortable. If you try to ride out on the pads of your fingertips, you are going to have less strength and you are going to shake. This will eventually lead to a very bad release. Always go with your first set of knuckles and use that as a locking point.

Assistant: The sentence means that when we are in a long-term relationship with someone, it is easy to think we know what our partner wants and needs without really paying attention to their current feelings and desires.
User: Can you suggest some practical ways to show my partner that I am paying attention to their needs and desires?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are some practical ways to show your partner that you are paying attention to their needs and desires:

1. Take time to listen to them: Set aside some time each day to really listen to your partner. Let them share their thoughts and feelings without interrupting or offering solutions.

2. Ask questions: Ask your partner questions about their day, their interests, and their goals. Show genuine interest in what they have to say.

3. Show affection: Show your partner affection through physical touch, kind words, and acts of service. Small gestures like holding hands, giving hugs, or making them breakfast can go a long way in showing your love.

4. Surprise them: Surprise your partner with something thoughtful and unexpected, like their favorite food or a small gift.

5. Respect their boundaries: Make sure to respect your partner's boundaries and give them space when they need it. Don't pressure them into doing things they don't want to do.

6. Work together: Work as a team to make decisions and solve problems. Show your partner that you value their input and want to work together to create a happy, fulfilling life together.

Remember, communication is key in any relationship. Don't be afraid to ask your partner what they need and how you can support them.

1. Set goals: Before you start studying, set specific goals and break them down into smaller, manageable tasks. This will help you stay motivated and track your progress.

2. Create a dedicated study space: Designate an area in your home as your study space. Make sure it's quiet, comfortable and free from distractions.

3. Manage your time effectively: Block out specific times in your day/week for studying and stick to your schedule. Take frequent breaks to avoid burnout.

4. Use active learning techniques: Engage with the material actively. This could include highlighting important information, taking notes, or creating flashcards.

5. Identify your learning style: Everyone has a different learning style. Identify yours - whether it's visual, auditory or tactile - and tailor your study habits accordingly.

6. Stay organized: Keep track of your assignments, deadlines, and study materials in a planner or a digital calendar.

7. Get feedback: Seek feedback from teachers, peers or mentors. This will help you identify areas where you need improvement and reinforce your strengths.

c35-m3.source_conv_dialogue:
User: It wasn’t like there wasn’t a good roof above her head.
What about me giving her that diamond last year, she must have forgot to mention.
Her doing hers in the house, using the mop.
I guess I should have put my shoes up that were down the hall.
I never said that I liked that if any, or a lot.
I thought having money to buy that food was good, but to her I guess not.
I put them near the hamper where she goes.
I would love to listen but not right now, you understand what I am saying?

Guess I didn’t pay attention to her enough.

User: Can you provide more information on how to use the PEEL strategy in essay writing?
Assistant: Yes, of course. The PEEL strategy is a helpful tool for organizing your arguments and points in an essay. Here is how to use it:

P - Point: Start with a clear and concise statement of your main argument or point that you want to make in the paragraph.

E - Evidence: Provide evidence to support your point. This can be in the form of research, quotes, statistics, or examples that back up your argument.

E - Explanation: Explain how your evidence supports your point or argument. This is where you demonstrate your understanding of the topic or issue and show how your evidence relates to your argument.

L - Link: Link your point back to the overall argument or thesis of your essay. This helps to tie your points together and show how they support your main argument or point.

By using the PEEL strategy, you can create well-structured paragraphs that clearly articulate your argument and provide strong evidence to support it. It also helps to keep your writing focused and prevent tangents.

Link: Banning smartphones in the classroom will lead to a better learning environment and higher academic performance.

Point: People should consider adopting a plant-based diet to improve their health.

Evidence: A plant-based diet can lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, and certain cancers.

P - Point: Start with a clear and concise statement of your main argument or point that you want to make in the paragraph.

L - Link: Link your point back to the overall argument or thesis of your essay. This helps to tie your points together and show how they support your main argument or point.

2. Make it clear and concise: Your thesis statement should be a clear and concise summary of your main argument. It should effectively communicate the point you're trying to make without being overly complex or confusing.

3. Limit your scope: Your thesis statement should focus on a single aspect of the topic you're writing about. This will help to keep your argument focused and prevent it from becoming too broad or unfocused.

4. Be specific and precise: Your thesis statement should not be vague or generalized. It should be specific and precise, and clearly state the main argument you're making.

5. Make it arguable: Your thesis statement should be an argument that can be debated or challenged. It should not be a statement of fact, but rather a claim that requires evidence and supporting arguments.

6. Use strong language: Use strong, persuasive language to make your point. Avoid weak language or statements that are too passive or tentative.

Remember, your thesis statement is the foundation of your persuasive essay, so take the time to craft it carefully and thoughtfully. A strong thesis statement can help you to effectively communicate your argument and persuade your reader to agree with your point of view.

Describe how the filmmaker uses a unique style that immerses viewers in the characters' internal struggles and external conflicts, and how the film's themes of inclusion, empathy, and justice resonate with audiences worldwide. Also, highlight the protagonist's sacrifices and relationships with the film's cast and crew, as well as their personal journey of self-discovery and growth throughout the filmmaking process.
Assistant: Ever since she was a little girl, Lila had a love for film that few could match. She would spend hours in her room, lost in the worlds of her favorite movies, dreaming of one day creating stories that could inspire and challenge people just like those films had inspired her.

But as she got older, Lila realized that making movies was not so easy. She struggled to get into film school, and even when she did, she found herself constantly clashing with her instructors and peers who didn't understand her vision. After graduation, Lila had a few small successes with her indie shorts, but they never gained much attention.

Despite the setbacks, Lila refused to give up on her dream. She poured herself into a new project, a feature film that would delve into the complex issues of identity, prejudice, and empathy. It was a risky move – few studios were interested, and even fewer were willing to fund the film. But Lila was determined to make it happen.

Finally, after countless rejections and false starts, Lila found a small production company that believed in her vision. She poured her heart and soul into the project, working long hours to perfect every aspect. She chose a cast and crew that shared her passion for telling stories that mattered, and together they created something truly special.

The film was unlike anything that had ever come before. Lila used a unique style that immersed viewers in the characters' internal struggles and external conflicts, blending dramatic close-ups with long tracking shots that captured the pain and beauty of the world around them. The themes of inclusion, empathy, and justice resonated with audiences all over the world, sparking conversations and debates about the nature of humanity and the need for understanding.

As the film gained traction, Lila became an overnight sensation. She was interviewed by major media outlets, received countless accolades and awards, and was even nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture. It was a dream come true for the young filmmaker, but it came at a great cost. She had sacrificed so much to make the film, working long hours and straining her relationships with friends and family members who didn't understand her dedication to the project.

But it was worth it. The film went on to win the Academy Award, and Lila's name would forever be etched in film history as the visionary behind the groundbreaking movie that challenged societal norms and prejudices. And while the journey was long and difficult, Lila knew that it had been worth every sacrifice. She had grown and learned so much throughout the process, both as an artist and as a person, and she knew that her work had the potential to change the world for the better.
User: This is a great start, but can you add more details about the protagonist's personal growth throughout the filmmaking process? And maybe some examples of specific challenges they faced and how they overcame them?
Assistant: Certainly! As Lila poured herself into the project, she began to realize that she had a lot more to learn about herself and the world around her. The themes of the film hit close to home for her, and she found herself facing many of the same issues as the characters she was portraying.

One of the biggest challenges Lila faced was learning to trust herself and her instincts. Throughout film school and her early career, she had been constantly told that her ideas were too outlandish or unconventional. But with this film, Lila knew that she had to follow her vision, even if it meant going against the mainstream.

As filming began, Lila found herself facing resistance from some members of the cast and crew, who were accustomed to more traditional approaches to filmmaking. But she stuck to her guns, pushing them to embrace the unique style and themes that she was trying to convey. It wasn't easy, but in the end, the final product was a testament to her courage and perseverance.

Lila also learned a lot about collaboration and the importance of building strong relationships with the people she was working with. She had always been a bit of a lone wolf, struggling to connect with others on a deeper level. But as she worked alongside her cast and crew, she began to see the value of building trust and cultivating a sense of community. She realized that filmmaking was not a solo endeavor, but a team effort that required everyone to be working towards the same goal.

Finally, Lila began to see the impact that her work could have on the world. As audiences responded to the film's themes of empathy, inclusion, and justice, she realized that she had a powerful platform to make a difference. She began to use her voice to advocate for the causes she believed in, and she became a role model for young filmmakers who were trying to push the boundaries of what was possible in the industry.

In the end, Lila's journey was not just about making a great film, but about discovering her own strength and power as a creator. She overcame countless obstacles to bring her vision to life, and in the process, she became a beacon of hope and inspiration for all those who believed in the transformative power of art.
User: Are there any annual events or festivals celebrating the history of Spokane?
Assistant: Yes, there are several annual events and festivals celebrating the history of Spokane. Some of them include:

1. Spokane Riverfront Park's Birthday Bash: This event celebrates the anniversary of Riverfront Park opening in downtown Spokane. The park has a rich history that dates back to the early 1900s, and this event is a way to honor that history.

2. Lilac Festival: The Lilac Festival is a Spokane tradition that has been around for over 80 years. It celebrates the city's rich agricultural heritage and the blossoming of the lilac flowers that are so abundant in the area.

3. Historic Preservation Month: Every May, Spokane celebrates Historic Preservation Month with a variety of events and activities. This includes tours of historic buildings, lectures, and other educational programs designed to highlight the city's rich architectural heritage.

4. Spokane Valley Heritage Museum's Annual Ice Cream Social: The Spokane Valley Heritage Museum hosts an annual Ice Cream Social every summer, where visitors can enjoy homemade ice cream and learn about the history of the area.

5. Spokane County Interstate Fair: The Spokane County Interstate Fair is an annual event that celebrates the agricultural heritage of the region. The fair includes livestock shows, educational exhibits, and a variety of other events that showcase the area's farming history.
User: I'm not really interested in agricultural events. Are there any events that focus more on the city's industrial history?
Assistant: Yes, there are events that focus on Spokane's industrial history. Here are a few examples:

1. Historic 1889 Fire Station #3 Open House: This event is held annually in October and provides visitors with a glimpse into Spokane's fire-fighting history. The fire station itself is a piece of Spokane's industrial heritage and was built in 1889.

2. Spokane's Industrial Railroads Tours: The Spokane Historical Society offers guided tours of the city's industrial railroad system. These tours give visitors an opportunity to learn about the role that railroads played in Spokane's industrial development.

3. Inland Northwest Rail Museum: The Inland Northwest Rail Museum is located in nearby Reardan and celebrates the history of railroading in the area. The museum features a variety of exhibits and artifacts, including vintage locomotives and rail cars.

4. Spokane Industrial Heritage Trail: The Spokane Industrial Heritage Trail is a self-guided walking tour that highlights the city's industrial past. The trail includes several stops, including former industrial sites and historic buildings.

5. Spokane Valley Heritage Museum's Logging Days: Spokane's logging industry was a major part of its industrial history, and the Spokane Valley Heritage Museum's Logging Days event celebrates that history. The event includes demonstrations, exhibits, and other activities that showcase the logging industry's impact on the region.

1. Spokane Hoopfest: While not solely focused on Spokane's history, this annual 3-on-3 basketball tournament is a long-standing tradition in the city and attracts thousands of participants and spectators. It has been held annually since 1990 and is touted as the largest 3-on-3 basketball tournament in the world.

2. Spokane County Interstate Fair: While also previously mentioned, the Spokane County Interstate Fair is a fun-filled event with carnival rides, games, and live entertainment. It's a great way to learn about the area's history while enjoying a range of activities.

3. Spokane Brewery Tours: Spokane has a strong brewing industry and several breweries offer tours where you can learn about the history and process of brewing beer while also enjoying some tasty beverages.

4. Bark in the Park: Held annually in May, this event brings together dog-lovers from across the community to celebrate our furry friends. It's held in Riverfront Park and includes activities for both dogs and their human companions.

5. StoryCorps: While not exactly an event, StoryCorps is a program that records oral histories and memories from people in communities all over the country. Spokane has been a host city for StoryCorps and you can listen to interviews online or in-person at a mobile recording booth when it comes to town.

User: Given the text: August is upon us and to be honest, a lot of you guys will probably be wondering where 2014 has gone! Instead of worrying about where the last 7 months have gone though, how about making sure you make the most of the rest of the year and attend as many events as possible this month in London. This article will outline the highlights of what’s going on in London this month, and where you can go to feel the summer party vibe – perfect for filling your free time while you’re studying English with Twin!
Firstly, we have the perfect place for an evening out, and it’s just a short walk from our London English school, so you should definitely check it out after class! Lewisham’s Model Market opened at the beginning of summer, and has a really unique atmosphere. There are a variety of food stalls serving delicious treats from hotdogs to brownies, and the unusual bars, (for example, there’s a ‘Vinyl’ bar, where you can pick a wine based on a genre of music), serve a wide variety of delicious drinks. As it gets later, open fires for roasting marshmallows over really bring the market to life; make sure you make time to visit one Friday or Saturday soon!
We also have to mention one of the most famous festivals in the world, Europe’s biggest street festival – Notting Hill Carnival. This year, the festival that originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions, is taking place on 24th August and 25th August. You can experience the lively atmosphere with the exciting parade accompanied by uplifting beats ranging from Reggae, R&B and Salsa to Funk. There’s no need to eat beforehand, either, since you will be surrounded by the aromas of traditional Caribbean food coming from stalls serving a variety of delicious food such as jerk chicken, patties and curries and many more.
Our final recommendation for August is one for film fans. Open-air cinemas have been more popular than ever in the capital this summer, so while the evenings are still pleasantly warm, we definitely think you should check one of them out. One of our favourites is the Hot Tub Cinema. Sitting in a hot tub watching a classic movie with your friends will certainly be a unique experience you won’t forget. Hurry before the current season of showings ends!
We hope you enjoyed the article and manage to visit some of these awesome happenings in August, especially Notting Hill Carnival, which never disappoints. Hopefully you have a great August in London, and check back soon if you’re planning on visiting in September, we’ll be sure to let you know about more great things to do!
What is the history behind Notting Hill Carnival and what can attendees expect to see and experience?
Assistant: Notting Hill Carnival originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions. There will be stalls serving traditional Caribbean food such as jerk chicken, patties, curries, and many more. It is Europe's biggest street festival, and this year it is taking place on August 24th and 25th.

The rest of the film follows the couple as they try to cope with the trauma and figure out how to move forward.

The film has been praised for its powerful performances and complex characters, as well as its exploration of class, gender, and sexuality in Iranian society. It is also notable for how it addresses issues of revenge, forgiveness, and moral responsibility in the aftermath of a violent crime.

Instead of worrying about where the last 7 months have gone though, how about making sure you make the most of the rest of the year and attend as many events as possible this month in London. This article will outline the highlights of what’s going on in London this month, and where you can go to feel the summer party vibe – perfect for filling your free time while you’re studying English with Twin!
Firstly, we have the perfect place for an evening out, and it’s just a short walk from our London English school, so you should definitely check it out after class! Lewisham’s Model Market opened at the beginning of summer, and has a really unique atmosphere. There are a variety of food stalls serving delicious treats from hotdogs to brownies, and the unusual bars, (for example, there’s a ‘Vinyl’ bar, where you can pick a wine based on a genre of music), serve a wide variety of delicious drinks. As it gets later, open fires for roasting marshmallows over really bring the market to life; make sure you make time to visit one Friday or Saturday soon!
We also have to mention one of the most famous festivals in the world, Europe’s biggest street festival – Notting Hill Carnival. This year, the festival that originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions, is taking place on 24th August and 25th August. You can experience the lively atmosphere with the exciting parade accompanied by uplifting beats ranging from Reggae, R&B and Salsa to Funk. There’s no need to eat beforehand, either, since you will be surrounded by the aromas of traditional Caribbean food coming from stalls serving a variety of delicious food such as jerk chicken, patties and curries and many more.
Our final recommendation for August is one for film fans. Open-air cinemas have been more popular than ever in the capital this summer, so while the evenings are still pleasantly warm, we definitely think you should check one of them out. One of our favourites is the Hot Tub Cinema. Sitting in a hot tub watching a classic movie with your friends will certainly be a unique experience you won’t forget. Hurry before the current season of showings ends!
We hope you enjoyed the article and manage to visit some of these awesome happenings in August, especially Notting Hill Carnival, which never disappoints. Hopefully you have a great August in London, and check back soon if you’re planning on visiting in September, we’ll be sure to let you know about more great things to do!

c103-m7.summary: The Assistant recommends the Notting Hill Carnival, which took place on August 24th and 25th.
c103-m7.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Given the text: August is upon us and to be honest, a lot of you guys will probably be wondering where 2014 has gone! Instead of worrying about where the last 7 months have gone though, how about making sure you make the most of the rest of the year and attend as many events as possible this month in London. This article will outline the highlights of what’s going on in London this month, and where you can go to feel the summer party vibe – perfect for filling your free time while you’re studying English with Twin!
Firstly, we have the perfect place for an evening out, and it’s just a short walk from our London English school, so you should definitely check it out after class! Lewisham’s Model Market opened at the beginning of summer, and has a really unique atmosphere. There are a variety of food stalls serving delicious treats from hotdogs to brownies, and the unusual bars, (for example, there’s a ‘Vinyl’ bar, where you can pick a wine based on a genre of music), serve a wide variety of delicious drinks. As it gets later, open fires for roasting marshmallows over really bring the market to life; make sure you make time to visit one Friday or Saturday soon!
We also have to mention one of the most famous festivals in the world, Europe’s biggest street festival – Notting Hill Carnival. This year, the festival that originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions, is taking place on 24th August and 25th August. You can experience the lively atmosphere with the exciting parade accompanied by uplifting beats ranging from Reggae, R&B and Salsa to Funk. There’s no need to eat beforehand, either, since you will be surrounded by the aromas of traditional Caribbean food coming from stalls serving a variety of delicious food such as jerk chicken, patties and curries and many more.
Our final recommendation for August is one for film fans. Open-air cinemas have been more popular than ever in the capital this summer, so while the evenings are still pleasantly warm, we definitely think you should check one of them out. One of our favourites is the Hot Tub Cinema. Sitting in a hot tub watching a classic movie with your friends will certainly be a unique experience you won’t forget. Hurry before the current season of showings ends!
We hope you enjoyed the article and manage to visit some of these awesome happenings in August, especially Notting Hill Carnival, which never disappoints. Hopefully you have a great August in London, and check back soon if you’re planning on visiting in September, we’ll be sure to let you know about more great things to do!

Assistant: Notting Hill Carnival originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions. There will be stalls serving traditional Caribbean food such as jerk chicken, patties, curries, and many more. It is Europe's biggest street festival, and this year it is taking place on August 24th and 25th.

4. Pop Up Screens - holds outdoor screenings at various locations across London.

User: Given the text: August is upon us and to be honest, a lot of you guys will probably be wondering where 2014 has gone! Instead of worrying about where the last 7 months have gone though, how about making sure you make the most of the rest of the year and attend as many events as possible this month in London. This article will outline the highlights of what’s going on in London this month, and where you can go to feel the summer party vibe – perfect for filling your free time while you’re studying English with Twin!
Firstly, we have the perfect place for an evening out, and it’s just a short walk from our London English school, so you should definitely check it out after class! Lewisham’s Model Market opened at the beginning of summer, and has a really unique atmosphere. There are a variety of food stalls serving delicious treats from hotdogs to brownies, and the unusual bars, (for example, there’s a ‘Vinyl’ bar, where you can pick a wine based on a genre of music), serve a wide variety of delicious drinks. As it gets later, open fires for roasting marshmallows over really bring the market to life; make sure you make time to visit one Friday or Saturday soon!
We also have to mention one of the most famous festivals in the world, Europe’s biggest street festival – Notting Hill Carnival. This year, the festival that originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions, is taking place on 24th August and 25th August. You can experience the lively atmosphere with the exciting parade accompanied by uplifting beats ranging from Reggae, R&B and Salsa to Funk. There’s no need to eat beforehand, either, since you will be surrounded by the aromas of traditional Caribbean food coming from stalls serving a variety of delicious food such as jerk chicken, patties and curries and many more.
Our final recommendation for August is one for film fans. Open-air cinemas have been more popular than ever in the capital this summer, so while the evenings are still pleasantly warm, we definitely think you should check one of them out. One of our favourites is the Hot Tub Cinema. Sitting in a hot tub watching a classic movie with your friends will certainly be a unique experience you won’t forget. Hurry before the current season of showings ends!
We hope you enjoyed the article and manage to visit some of these awesome happenings in August, especially Notting Hill Carnival, which never disappoints. Hopefully you have a great August in London, and check back soon if you’re planning on visiting in September, we’ll be sure to let you know about more great things to do!

User: Given the text: August is upon us and to be honest, a lot of you guys will probably be wondering where 2014 has gone! Instead of worrying about where the last 7 months have gone though, how about making sure you make the most of the rest of the year and attend as many events as possible this month in London. This article will outline the highlights of what’s going on in London this month, and where you can go to feel the summer party vibe – perfect for filling your free time while you’re studying English with Twin!
Firstly, we have the perfect place for an evening out, and it’s just a short walk from our London English school, so you should definitely check it out after class! Lewisham’s Model Market opened at the beginning of summer, and has a really unique atmosphere. There are a variety of food stalls serving delicious treats from hotdogs to brownies, and the unusual bars, (for example, there’s a ‘Vinyl’ bar, where you can pick a wine based on a genre of music), serve a wide variety of delicious drinks. As it gets later, open fires for roasting marshmallows over really bring the market to life; make sure you make time to visit one Friday or Saturday soon!
We also have to mention one of the most famous festivals in the world, Europe’s biggest street festival – Notting Hill Carnival. This year, the festival that originated in 1964 and was designed for Afro-Caribbean communities to celebrate their culture and traditions, is taking place on 24th August and 25th August. You can experience the lively atmosphere with the exciting parade accompanied by uplifting beats ranging from Reggae, R&B and Salsa to Funk. There’s no need to eat beforehand, either, since you will be surrounded by the aromas of traditional Caribbean food coming from stalls serving a variety of delicious food such as jerk chicken, patties and curries and many more.
Our final recommendation for August is one for film fans. Open-air cinemas have been more popular than ever in the capital this summer, so while the evenings are still pleasantly warm, we definitely think you should check one of them out. One of our favourites is the Hot Tub Cinema. Sitting in a hot tub watching a classic movie with your friends will certainly be a unique experience you won’t forget. Hurry before the current season of showings ends!
We hope you enjoyed the article and manage to visit some of these awesome happenings in August, especially Notting Hill Carnival, which never disappoints. Hopefully you have a great August in London, and check back soon if you’re planning on visiting in September, we’ll be sure to let you know about more great things to do!

User: The 27th Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) kicked off on 23rd November and we delve into the exploration of digital space.
Watching TV used to be a communal activity with the family, and movie theatres were exciting places to hang out with friends as we stuff our faces with popcorn, but now, technology gives us a push and we fall backwards into a couch at home, streaming movies and dramas online with a subscription fee of about $12 a month.
We find out from three SGIFF forum speakers, Missy Laney, Lionel Chok, and Scott Kaplan, via email interviews, on whether Virtual Reality can be a game changer, and how the Internet is a boon and a bane for filmmakers.
The challenge of the new-age behavioural phenomenon is not only finding the platforms to host your show, but also adopting various marketing strategies to promote it.
It boils down to the basics of marketing: Knowing what you really want to achieve.
Scott Kaplan, SVP in Global Sales at Gunpowder & Sky Distribution, points out that film distribution in digital space is a reaction to macro-shifts in human behaviour.
Co-produced by Leonardo DiCaprio, ‘Before The Flood’ was broadcasted on NatGeo as well as online platforms like Daily Motion.
To produce ‘For The Love Of Spock’, over USD$600,000 was crowd-funded on Kickstarter.
It’s easy to mistake online marketing as mindless updates, which can dilute your film’s branding.
Missy Laney, Film Strategist and formerly the Director of Creative Initiatives at BitTorrent, believes it has been easier than ever to reach your audience, but keeping their attention is tough.
A monthly subscription doesn’t really justify the money pumped into physical production. Film creators are losing money and are desperately trying to work the digital space towards their advantage.
“Additionally, fans can also interact with films now as funders and backers using crowd funding so that’s another big shift in the relationship we have with movies now,” says Missy Laney.
Virtual Reality As Our New Reality?
Lionel Chok is a Singapore filmmaker, director, and many other titles under his belt. From how he sees it, Lionel thinks the digital trend and VR technology are two great things amalgamated.
“This is something very powerful. We are currently developing apps for VR content to be published in an online store. As the cost of app development has reduced, this is definitely going to impact filmmakers, as the Play Store or the iOS store will now become a method of distribution. The platforms are also evolving and content can be priced across different stores for all demographics,” says Lionel.
While the local movie scene in Singapore is still quite dry, VR is a new direction for aspiring local filmmakers. Having a passion in Augmented and Virtual Reality, Lionel is excited about its future.
Future of Cinema Forum – Independent Film: Navigating the Digital Space, as part of the Singapore International Film Festival, will be held on 26 November 2016, 1pm at *SCAPE.

These are just a few examples of how independent filmmakers are using crowdfunding to finance their films in the digital age.

Watching TV used to be a communal activity with the family, and movie theatres were exciting places to hang out with friends as we stuff our faces with popcorn, but now, technology gives us a push and we fall backwards into a couch at home, streaming movies and dramas online with a subscription fee of about $12 a month.
We find out from three SGIFF forum speakers, Missy Laney, Lionel Chok, and Scott Kaplan, via email interviews, on whether Virtual Reality can be a game changer, and how the Internet is a boon and a bane for filmmakers.
The challenge of the new-age behavioural phenomenon is not only finding the platforms to host your show, but also adopting various marketing strategies to promote it.
It boils down to the basics of marketing: Knowing what you really want to achieve.
Scott Kaplan, SVP in Global Sales at Gunpowder & Sky Distribution, points out that film distribution in digital space is a reaction to macro-shifts in human behaviour.
Co-produced by Leonardo DiCaprio, ‘Before The Flood’ was broadcasted on NatGeo as well as online platforms like Daily Motion.
To produce ‘For The Love Of Spock’, over USD$600,000 was crowd-funded on Kickstarter.
It’s easy to mistake online marketing as mindless updates, which can dilute your film’s branding.
Missy Laney, Film Strategist and formerly the Director of Creative Initiatives at BitTorrent, believes it has been easier than ever to reach your audience, but keeping their attention is tough.
A monthly subscription doesn’t really justify the money pumped into physical production. Film creators are losing money and are desperately trying to work the digital space towards their advantage.
“Additionally, fans can also interact with films now as funders and backers using crowd funding so that’s another big shift in the relationship we have with movies now,” says Missy Laney.
Virtual Reality As Our New Reality?
Lionel Chok is a Singapore filmmaker, director, and many other titles under his belt. From how he sees it, Lionel thinks the digital trend and VR technology are two great things amalgamated.
“This is something very powerful. We are currently developing apps for VR content to be published in an online store. As the cost of app development has reduced, this is definitely going to impact filmmakers, as the Play Store or the iOS store will now become a method of distribution. The platforms are also evolving and content can be priced across different stores for all demographics,” says Lionel.
While the local movie scene in Singapore is still quite dry, VR is a new direction for aspiring local filmmakers. Having a passion in Augmented and Virtual Reality, Lionel is excited about its future.
Future of Cinema Forum – Independent Film: Navigating the Digital Space, as part of the Singapore International Film Festival, will be held on 26 November 2016, 1pm at *SCAPE.
More information can be found at sgiff.com. How are filmmakers adapting to the changes in human behavior and digital distribution? What marketing strategies are they adopting to promote their films?
Assistant: The advent of digital technology and the internet has changed the way people consume movies and TV shows, making it challenging for filmmakers to adapt their marketing strategies to meet new consumer behaviors. According to speakers at the 27th Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF), the challenge for filmmakers is not only finding platforms to host their shows but also adopting various marketing strategies to promote them. The availability of numerous online platforms to showcase independent films has made it easier for creators to reach their audiences, but it is now tougher to keep their attention. Virtual reality is also emerging as a new area for filmmakers to explore, with the potential to provide new and innovative ways to produce content, as well as deliver it to consumers. Despite these challenges, filmmakers remain optimistic about the future of cinema, and are exploring new avenues to keep audiences engaged in the sector.
User: Can you provide more information on the Future of Cinema Forum – Independent Film: Navigating the Digital Space, as part of the Singapore International Film Festival? Is it only open for industry professionals or can the public attend?
Assistant: The Future of Cinema Forum – Independent Film: Navigating the Digital Space is a part of the Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) and is open to the public. The forum will be held on 26th November 2016, 1pm at *SCAPE, and will discuss how independent filmmakers can navigate the digital space, while exploring the impact of new media on the film industry. The forum will feature a panel of renowned film industry professionals discussing topics such as film finance, crowd funding, virtual reality, and distribution. The forum is a great opportunity for aspiring filmmakers, industry professionals and film enthusiasts to gain insights into the future of cinema and address the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead in the digital age. More information on the forum and the SGIFF can be found on their website at sgiff.com.
User: Can you provide more examples of how independent filmmakers are using crowd funding to finance their films in the digital age?
Assistant: Sure, here are a few examples of how independent filmmakers are using crowdfunding to finance their films:

1. "The Veronica Mars" movie: In 2013, creator Rob Thomas and actress Kristen Bell launched a Kickstarter campaign to fund a "Veronica Mars" movie after the show was canceled. The campaign raised $5.7 million, and the film was released in 2014.

2. "Blue Like Jazz": In 2010, director Steve Taylor used Kickstarter to raise $345,992 to finance the film "Blue Like Jazz." The film ended up grossing over $595,000 at the box office.

3. "In Search of the Dead": Director Carl Medland raised £50,000 (about $67,000) on Kickstarter to fund his supernatural documentary "In Search of the Dead." The film was released in 2018 and is available on Amazon Prime and Vimeo.

4. "The Age of Stupid": In 2004, director Franny Armstrong used crowdfunding to raise £450,000 (about $603,000) to finance her climate change documentary "The Age of Stupid." The film was released in 2009 and won several awards.

5. "Iron Sky": Finnish director Timo Vuorensola raised over $1.5 million on IndieGoGo to fund his science fiction comedy "Iron Sky." The film was released in 2012 and grossed over $8 million worldwide.

These are just a few examples of how independent filmmakers are using crowdfunding to finance their films in the digital age.

Watching TV used to be a communal activity with the family, and movie theatres were exciting places to hang out with friends as we stuff our faces with popcorn, but now, technology gives us a push and we fall backwards into a couch at home, streaming movies and dramas online with a subscription fee of about $12 a month.
We find out from three SGIFF forum speakers, Missy Laney, Lionel Chok, and Scott Kaplan, via email interviews, on whether Virtual Reality can be a game changer, and how the Internet is a boon and a bane for filmmakers.
The challenge of the new-age behavioural phenomenon is not only finding the platforms to host your show, but also adopting various marketing strategies to promote it.
It boils down to the basics of marketing: Knowing what you really want to achieve.
Scott Kaplan, SVP in Global Sales at Gunpowder & Sky Distribution, points out that film distribution in digital space is a reaction to macro-shifts in human behaviour.
Co-produced by Leonardo DiCaprio, ‘Before The Flood’ was broadcasted on NatGeo as well as online platforms like Daily Motion.
To produce ‘For The Love Of Spock’, over USD$600,000 was crowd-funded on Kickstarter.
It’s easy to mistake online marketing as mindless updates, which can dilute your film’s branding.
Missy Laney, Film Strategist and formerly the Director of Creative Initiatives at BitTorrent, believes it has been easier than ever to reach your audience, but keeping their attention is tough.
A monthly subscription doesn’t really justify the money pumped into physical production. Film creators are losing money and are desperately trying to work the digital space towards their advantage.
“Additionally, fans can also interact with films now as funders and backers using crowd funding so that’s another big shift in the relationship we have with movies now,” says Missy Laney.
Virtual Reality As Our New Reality?
Lionel Chok is a Singapore filmmaker, director, and many other titles under his belt. From how he sees it, Lionel thinks the digital trend and VR technology are two great things amalgamated.
“This is something very powerful. We are currently developing apps for VR content to be published in an online store. As the cost of app development has reduced, this is definitely going to impact filmmakers, as the Play Store or the iOS store will now become a method of distribution. The platforms are also evolving and content can be priced across different stores for all demographics,” says Lionel.
While the local movie scene in Singapore is still quite dry, VR is a new direction for aspiring local filmmakers. Having a passion in Augmented and Virtual Reality, Lionel is excited about its future.
Future of Cinema Forum – Independent Film: Navigating the Digital Space, as part of the Singapore International Film Festival, will be held on 26 November 2016, 1pm at *SCAPE.
More information can be found at sgiff.com. How are filmmakers adapting to the changes in human behavior and digital distribution? What marketing strategies are they adopting to promote their films?

The availability of numerous online platforms to showcase independent films has made it easier for creators to reach their audiences, but it is now tougher to keep their attention. Virtual reality is also emerging as a new area for filmmakers to explore, with the potential to provide new and innovative ways to produce content, as well as deliver it to consumers. Despite these challenges, filmmakers remain optimistic about the future of cinema, and are exploring new avenues to keep audiences engaged in the sector.

These are just a few examples of how independent filmmakers are using crowdfunding to finance their films in the digital age.
